info.text: Unit 3 — Raising a defect in the tech log. B2. Listening, reading, use of English and vocabulary.

questiontext.text: Listen to Dialogue 1 again. The mechanic turns the vague pilot report into a clear tech-log entry. Which line does the mechanic finally write?

generalfeedback.text: The entry records the observed symptom in the present perfect: "The left brake pedal has felt soft during landing." It names the symptom and avoids naming a cause.

answer.text: The left brake pedal has felt soft during landing.

feedback.text: Correct — the observed symptom, in the present perfect.

answer.text: The brake seal has failed and must be replaced now.

feedback.text: No — a failed seal is an assumption about the cause, not an observation.

answer.text: Something feels wrong with the brakes in the flight.

feedback.text: No — that is the vague pilot report the mechanic replaced.

answer.text: The left main gear brake has stopped working fully.

feedback.text: No — nobody observed a total loss of braking; the pedal only felt soft.

name.text: U03 L2 — Dialogue 1 observation vs assumption

questiontext.text: Listen to Dialogue 1 again. The mechanic records "the seal has failed" as the observation in the tech log.

generalfeedback.text: False. "The seal has failed" is called an assumption, not an observation. Only what was seen — a soft pedal — is recorded.

feedback.text: No — the mechanic explicitly calls that an assumption.
Correct — it is an assumption; only the observed symptom is recorded.

questiontext.text: Listen to Dialogue 2 again. The mechanic reports three findings on the brake unit. Which set is correct?

generalfeedback.text: The three observed findings are a hydraulic leak at the union, chafing where the line rubs a bracket, and play in the wheel bearing.

answer.text: A hydraulic leak, chafing, and bearing play.

feedback.text: Correct — leak, chafing and play, each with a location.

answer.text: A crack, light corrosion, and a soft brake pedal.

feedback.text: No — a soft pedal is the pilot's symptom, not a finding on the unit.

answer.text: A leak, a blank display, and a stored code.

feedback.text: No — the blank display and stored code belong to Dialogue 3.

answer.text: Corrosion, a loose plug, and low oil pressure.

feedback.text: No — those items do not all appear in Dialogue 2.

name.text: U03 L4 — Dialogue 3 why hard to find

questiontext.text: Listen to Dialogue 3 again. Why is the display fault hard to find on the ground?

generalfeedback.text: The fault is intermittent — it comes and goes — so it does not show on the ground. That is why they run the BITE for a stored code.

answer.text: It is intermittent, so it comes and goes.

feedback.text: Correct — an intermittent fault is not present all the time.

answer.text: The BITE cannot store any fault code at all.

feedback.text: No — the BITE did store a code from the last flight.

answer.text: The display is broken and never switches on.

feedback.text: No — on the ground the display works.

answer.text: The data bus has been removed from the whole unit.

feedback.text: No — the bus is present; a fault was logged on it.

questiontext.text: Listen to the shift-handover voicemail (Dialogue 4) again. How many defects were recorded in the tech log? Write the number.

generalfeedback.text: Three: the leak, the chafing, and the bearing play.

feedback.text: Correct — leak, chafing and play.
Listen again — the lead lists three defects.

questiontext.text: Listen to the voicemail (Dialogue 4) again. What tech-log reference number is given for the recorded defects?

generalfeedback.text: Reference 5182. Catching spoken numbers exactly is a real line-station skill.

feedback.text: Correct — reference 5182.
Listen again for the four-digit reference number.

questiontext.text: Listen to the voicemail (Dialogue 4) again. Which stand is the handover for? Write the number.

generalfeedback.text: Stand 9.

feedback.text: Correct — stand 9.
Listen again — the handover names one stand.

questiontext.text:
Read this work order.

WORK ORDER 7731. Remove and replace the left brake line. Torque the union to the AMM value. Refill and bleed the hydraulic system. Function-test the brakes before release.

What must be done before the aircraft is released?

generalfeedback.text: The last step is a function test of the brakes before release.

feedback.text: Correct — the brakes are function-tested before release.

answer.text: Order a new borescope from stores.

feedback.text: No — the order does not mention a borescope.

answer.text: Sign the aircraft into service at once.

feedback.text: No — release comes only after the function test.

answer.text: Leave the union only finger-tight for now.

feedback.text: No — the union is torqued to the AMM value.

questiontext.text:
Read this AMM caution.

AMM 32-41 CAUTION: Do not exceed the torque value for the union. Over-torque can crack the fitting.

The caution warns that over-torque can crack the fitting.

generalfeedback.text: True — the caution states that over-torque can crack the fitting, so you must not exceed the value.

feedback.text: Correct — that is exactly what the caution says.
Read again — the caution links over-torque to a cracked fitting.

questiontext.text:
Read this service bulletin extract.

SB-32-118: Inspect the brake line for chafing where it passes the bracket. If chafing is found, install the protective sleeve. Chafing that has worn through the line requires line replacement.

What do you install if chafing is found (but the line is not worn through)?

generalfeedback.text: A protective sleeve. The line is only replaced if the chafing has worn through it.

feedback.text: Correct — the sleeve protects the line from further chafing.
No — the bulletin is about the brake line, not the bearing.
No — a new line is needed only if the line is worn through.
No — no borescope is fitted; the sleeve is installed.

questiontext.text:
Read this airworthiness directive extract.

AD-2026-07: A repetitive borescope inspection of the housing is required every 200 flight hours until the modified part is fitted.

The AD requires the borescope inspection to be repeated.

generalfeedback.text: True — "repetitive ... every 200 flight hours" means the inspection is repeated until the modified part is fitted.

feedback.text: Correct — a repetitive inspection is repeated at set intervals.
Read again — "repetitive" means it must be repeated.

questiontext.text: Read the AD extract again: "A repetitive borescope inspection of the housing is required every 200 flight hours." After how many flight hours must the inspection be repeated?

generalfeedback.text: Every 200 flight hours.

feedback.text: Correct — 200 flight hours.
Read the interval again — it is stated in flight hours.

questiontext.text:
Complete with the present perfect of the verb in brackets. Write two words.

The panel ___ (develop) cracks.

generalfeedback.text: has developed — the cracks are still there now, so use has/have + the past participle.

feedback.text: Correct.
Use has + the past participle: has developed.

questiontext.text:
Complete with the correct past participle.

I have ___ (find) a hydraulic leak at the union.

generalfeedback.text: found — "find" is irregular: find / found / found.

feedback.text: Correct — the participle of find is found.
Irregular verb: find / found / found.

questiontext.text:
Write for or since.

The valve has leaked ___ two flights.

generalfeedback.text: for — use "for" with a length of time (two flights).

feedback.text: Correct — "for" + a length of time.
Two flights is a length of time, so use "for".

questiontext.text:
Write for or since.

The line has leaked ___ yesterday.

generalfeedback.text: since — use "since" with a start point (yesterday).

feedback.text: Correct — "since" + a start point.
Yesterday is a start point, so use "since".

questiontext.text:
Make the sentence negative in the present perfect. Write three words for the gap.

The technician ___ ___ ___ the leak yet. (not / rectify)

generalfeedback.text: has not rectified — negative present perfect is has/have + not + past participle.

feedback.text: Correct.
Correct — the contracted form is fine.
Use has + not + participle: has not rectified.

name.text: U03 U6 — rephrase the pilot (bank term)

questiontext.text: Complete with one bank term. The pilot says the display "goes off, then comes back". In technical terms the fault is ___.

generalfeedback.text: intermittent — a fault that comes and goes.

feedback.text: Correct — an intermittent fault comes and goes.
A fault that comes and goes is intermittent.

name.text: U03 V1 — term to plain meaning

questiontext.text: Match each defect-description term to its plain meaning.

generalfeedback.text: leak = escaping fluid; chafing = rubbing damage; corrosion = chemical damage; play = loose movement; wear = loss of material from use.

partiallycorrectfeedback.text: Some matches are right — check the rest against the vocabulary bank.

incorrectfeedback.text: Review the vocabulary bank and try again.

answer.text: fluid escaping where it should not
rubbing damage where two parts touch
chemical damage that eats the metal
loose free movement in a bearing
gradual loss of material from use

name.text: U03 V2 — term to word partner

questiontext.text: Match each term to the phrase it is normally used in.

generalfeedback.text: Terms are learned inside their word partner: raise a snag, run the BITE, use a borescope, enter in the tech log, declare it unserviceable.

partiallycorrectfeedback.text: Some are right — check the collocations again.

incorrectfeedback.text: Review the word partners in the vocabulary bank.

questiontext.text: Which term means "a fault that comes and goes"?

generalfeedback.text: intermittent. Corrosion, chafing and "unserviceable" describe other things.

feedback.text: Correct — it comes and goes.
No — that means not safe or allowed to be used.
No — that is chemical damage to the metal.
No — that is rubbing damage where two parts touch.

questiontext.text: Which verb is normally used with "a defect" when the crew first reports it?

generalfeedback.text: You raise a defect (or a snag). You later rectify it; a borescope and a placard are tools and actions, not this verb.

feedback.text: Correct — raise a defect / raise a snag.
No — you rectify a defect later, when you repair it.
No — a borescope is an inspection tool, not this verb.
No — you placard an unserviceable unit; you do not "placard a defect" when reporting it.
